content.text: Public trust is not produced by slogans. It depends on the {{gap:1}} (RELY) of information, the {{gap:2}} (TRANSPARENT) of decision-making and the ability of officials to respond {{gap:3}} (RESPOND) when mistakes occur. In a crisis, citizens also notice whether an institution can explain a {{gap:4}} (CONSISTENT) between its public promise and its practical action without resorting to technical language. An apparently minor {{gap:5}} (ADMIT) of uncertainty may strengthen credibility, because it shows that an institution is not {{gap:6}} (CONCERN) with protecting its image at any cost. Citizens are more likely to remain {{gap:7}} (SUPPORT) when explanations are clear, policies are {{gap:8}} (PREDICT), and corrections are made before suspicion becomes harder to reverse. This combination of candour and consistency is difficult to maintain, but it gives citizens a basis for judging future announcements. Trust grows when institutions make the reasoning behind a change visible to those affected.

questions.explanation: The noun reliability is required after the.
Transparency is the noun naming an open process.
Inconsistency is the noun for a lack of consistency.
Admission is the noun after an.
Concerned is the adjective used with be.
Supportive is the adjective after remain.
